meta.subtitle: Electrical connection and protection maker growing fast on infrastructure and data-center demand; the share price already reflects most of it.

analystCommentary: We rate nVent Electric HOLD with a $160 to $205 target range. The business is growing quickly. Second-quarter 2026 sales rose by about half year over year, mostly organically, and management credits the infrastructure vertical, which includes its data-center business. The difficulty is the price. The shares already trade at a rich multiple of current-year consensus earnings, and consensus expects a smaller revenue step in FY27E than in FY26E. Our Base case lets that multiple compress modestly as growth slows, which leaves fair value only a little above the price. Our Bear case prices a stall in earnings at a lower multiple. The call is close in both directions, and the valuation section shows what would move it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: nVent Electric plc designs, manufactures, markets, installs and services electrical connection and protection solutions. It was founded in 1903 and is based in London, the United Kingdom. It reports two segments, Systems Protection and Electrical Connections, which represented approximately 72% and 28% of total revenues in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Its brands include nVent CADDY, ERICO, HOFFMAN, ILSCO, SCHROFF and TRACHTE, and its products serve industrial, commercial and residential, infrastructure and energy applications, including data centers. The portfolio changed in 2025. On January 30, 2025 nVent sold its Thermal Management business to an affiliate of funds managed by Brookfield Asset Management for $1.6 billion in net cash proceeds, subject to customary purchase price adjustments; that business is now reported as discontinued operations. On May 1, 2025 it bought the enclosures, switchgear and bus systems businesses of Avail Infrastructure Solutions, the Electrical Products Group, for approximately $1.0 billion, funded with cash on hand and operated predominantly within Systems Protection. FY25 revenue was $3.9 billion.

thesis.body: Management says the electrification, sustainability and digitalization megatrends, including the increased use of artificial intelligence, have led to sales growth, particularly in the infrastructure vertical that holds its data-center business, and it expects them to keep driving growth through 2026 and beyond. The second-quarter results bear that out: growth was mostly organic and operating margin widened. Two things hold us back. The margin gain came from spreading SG&A over higher sales and from restructuring savings, while gross margin fell on inflation, unfavorable mix and capacity investment, so it depends on volume staying high. And the price already pays a rich multiple on current-year consensus earnings while consensus expects growth to slow. We think fair value sits only modestly above the price, so the shares are a HOLD, by a narrow margin.

catalysts: Third-quarter 2026 results: the Electrical Products Group closed on May 1, 2025, so its comparison effect should largely fall away and give a cleaner read on organic growth.
Data-center and power-utility demand: management expects the megatrends behind its infrastructure growth to continue through 2026 and beyond.
Operating leverage: if volumes hold, further SG&A leverage and restructuring savings could keep operating margin rising despite gross-margin pressure.
Capital deployment: acquisitions and strategic capital deployment are among management's 2026 operating objectives, and a well-priced deal could extend the infrastructure exposure.
risks: Valuation: the shares price continued fast growth, so a slowdown would likely cost multiple as well as earnings.
Growth concentration: most organic growth came from the infrastructure business, so a pause in data-center or utility spending would hit hard.
Gross-margin pressure: inflation, tariffs, mix and capacity investment have pushed gross margin down while sales rose.
Cash conversion: free cash flow fell in FY25 on the statement table, and the sources disagree on its level.
Cyclicality: the 10-K ties demand to the global economy, capital spending and interest rates.

financials.incomeCommentary: Second-quarter 2026 net sales were $1,471.3 million, {+ up 52.8% +} from $963.1 million a year earlier. Gross margin was 37.9%, {- down 0.7 points -} from 38.6%; the company attributes the decline to inflation in raw materials and labor, unfavorable product mix and investments in capacity, partly offset by volume leverage and productivity. Gross profit also included approximately $25 million of IEEPA tariff reimbursements, which the company says were offset by other incremental tariffs. SG&A fell 4.6 points as a share of sales, which the company credits to leverage on fixed expenses and restructuring savings, even as intangible amortization rose to $41.1 million from $35.9 million as a result of the acquisition. Operating income was $300.7 million, a 20.4% margin, {+ up 4.1 points +} from 16.3%. Net income from continuing operations rose 102.2% to $215.8 million, with the effective tax rate up to 23.5% from 22.7%, partly on $3.6 million of tax expense from a foreign tax audit settlement. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, net sales were $2,713.3 million, {+ up 53.1% +}, operating margin was 18.3% against 16.2%, and gross margin fell 1.7 points to 37.0%. Six-month net income fell 23.8% to $358.3 million because the prior-year half carried $276.5 million of discontinued-operations income, primarily the gain on the Thermal Management sale; income from continuing operations rose 83.9%. On the annual table, revenue grew in each of the last three years, by 29.5% in FY25, but gross margin fell to 37.7% from 40.2% in FY24 and operating margin to 15.8% from 17.5%; the page gives no explanation for the FY25 decline. Two sources disagree on FY25 EPS. The table shows diluted EPS of $4.31 on net income of $710.2 million, while the proxy reports EPS from continuing operations of $2.60, up 82% from $1.43. The table is not on the proxy's continuing-operations basis, so we use the proxy figure for the ongoing earnings base.
financials.balanceCommentary: Total debt was $1.6 billion at FY25, down from $2.2 billion at FY24, against total equity of $3.7 billion. The table shows no cash or net-debt figure for FY24 or FY25, so the page cannot tell us how much of the Thermal Management proceeds remained after the acquisition, and we do not label the company net cash or net debt. The current ratio was 1.63 at FY25 and 1.80 on a trailing basis. Second-quarter net interest expense was $17.4 million against $17.6 million a year earlier, small beside the quarter's operating income. The page shows no interest-coverage or net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio, so our leverage read rests on the debt and equity figures alone, and on those figures the balance sheet does not constrain the growth plan.
financials.cashflowCommentary: On the statement table, FY25 operating cash flow was $0.5 billion against $0.6 billion in FY24, and free cash flow was $371.9 million after $93.3 million of capital expenditure, an FCF margin of 9.6%, {- down from 18.9% -} in FY24. The proxy gives different figures for 2025: net cash provided by operating activities of $649 million and total Free Cash Flow of $561 million, a company-defined measure, and it says cash flow grew at or above 30% in 2025. The page does not reconcile the two sources, and we use the statement table. nVent paid $253.1 million for share repurchases and $130.4 million in dividends in FY25, in line with the approximately $383 million the proxy says it returned to shareholders and more than the table's free cash flow. The trailing FCF yield is 2.2% and the dividend yield 0.52%, so the return case rests on earnings growth rather than cash returned.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $162.85 the shares trade at 44.4x trailing earnings, 26.9x trailing EV/EBITDA and 5.5x sales. The page labels its 31.7x forward multiple as next twelve months, but that figure matches the price over FY26E consensus EPS of $5.14, so we read it as the current-year multiple and use it as the like-for-like reference. The 25.1x on FY27E EPS of $6.48 is today's price over next year's earnings, not a multiple the shares will trade on a year out. The pack carries no peer multiples and no history of nVent's own multiple, so we do not call the current-year multiple a premium or a discount to anything; we judge it against growth. Consensus EPS rises between the two years while the revenue step narrows (see Growth). The Street is more bullish than we are: 16 of 17 analysts rate the shares Buy, with a $206.67 consensus target, a $210.00 median and a $136.00 to $240.00 range. The shares sit below the $184.64 52-week high and far above the $93.22 low, and no source on the page explains either move.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Organic growth stays strong after the acquisition comparison fades and operating margin keeps rising, so the shares hold today's 31.7x current-year multiple a year out. We apply 32x, that multiple rounded, to FY27E consensus EPS of $6.48. The result sits next to the $206.67 consensus target, so our Bull is roughly the Street's central case.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus FY27E EPS is delivered, but as revenue growth slows from FY26E the market pays 28x on it, a modest compression from today's current-year multiple. Slipping gross margin and the end of the acquisition contribution argue against holding the multiple; organic growth this strong argues against a deeper cut.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Data-center and infrastructure spending cools, gross margin keeps falling under inflation and tariffs, and FY27E growth does not arrive, leaving earnings near FY26E consensus EPS of $5.14. The multiple falls to 25x, about the 25.1x the price now puts on FY27E earnings, because earnings that stop growing would not keep today's current-year multiple.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting Bull 25%, Base 50% and Bear 25% gives an expected upside of +7.3% and a bear-case downside of -21.1%, a reward/risk of 0.34×, which derives HOLD. The Base carries half the weight because it is where the consensus numbers point once growth slows. Bull and Bear carry equal weight because the evidence cuts both ways: organic growth and the operating-margin gain on one side; slipping gross margin, a fading acquisition contribution and a lower FY25 free-cash-flow margin on the other. The call is close. A Base multiple held nearer today's current-year multiple would derive BUY, and so would moving ten points of weight from Bear to Bull; a Base at 25x, or ten points moved the other way, leaves HOLD. A fall back toward the 52-week low is a tail outside the Bear, not a reason to raise its weight. The $160 to $205 target range brackets the Base and stops just short of the Bull.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The pack shows a single reportable segment, but the 10-Q reports two, and we follow the 10-Q. Systems Protection, the larger by revenue, sells enclosures, liquid and air cooling, control buildings, switchgear systems and power distribution that protect electronics, systems and data in mission critical applications, including data centers; the company says its data-center business sits primarily in this segment, and the Electrical Products Group is operated predominantly within it. Electrical Connections sells bus systems, cable management, electrical connections and power connections across commercial and residential, infrastructure and industrial verticals, and the company says its offerings reduce installation time. The excerpt gives no segment sales or segment income, so we cannot say which segment drove the margin gain.

moatFactors.name: Brand portfolio
moatFactors.body: Some of nVent's brands have a history spanning over 100 years, according to the March 2026 proxy, and they support the reputation for quality and reliability that the 10-K lists among the bases of competition. Brands alone do not stop price competition, which the 10-K says can intensify in downturns.

moatFactors.name: Installed position in critical applications
moatFactors.body: The 10-K lists technical expertise, timeliness of delivery and previous installation history alongside price as bases of competition. Where nVent's products protect mission critical equipment in data centers and infrastructure, an installation history can favor the incumbent on the next project. The same 10-K warns that some competitors compete primarily on price, localized expertise and local relationships.

moatFactors.name: Scale and breadth
moatFactors.body: A portfolio running from enclosures and cooling to connections and switchgear lets nVent serve customers whose demand the 10-K calls often global in scope but localized in delivery. The same filing says nVent competes with thousands of smaller regional and local companies that may produce at lower cost, so breadth helps on global accounts but does not shield local business from cheaper rivals.

moatFactors.name: Pricing
moatFactors.body: The company counts selective increases in selling prices within its organic growth, yet gross margin still fell in the second quarter and the six months on the inflation, mix and capacity costs it cites. Pricing has not offset those pressures, so we do not treat it as a strong defense yet.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. The 10-K describes highly competitive, geographically diverse markets with large, well-established global rivals, lower-cost manufacturers and possible new entrants, and it warns that downturns could push competitors to compete more aggressively on price. Against that, an installed position in mission critical applications and long-standing brands give some protection, and the demand tailwind management describes is strong. A tailwind is not a moat: if data-center spending slows, the competitive pressures the 10-K describes would weigh more heavily. Durability also depends on integrating acquisitions, a risk named in both the 10-K and the 10-Q's forward-looking statements.

points: Second-quarter 2026 growth split into 46.9 points organic, 5.4 points from the acquisition and 0.5 points from currency; for the six months the split was 41.2, 10.7 and 1.2 points.

The infrastructure business contributed approximately 44.0 points of second-quarter organic growth and commercial and residential approximately 2.0 points; the company says this includes selective increases in selling prices and growth in the data-centers business.

The Electrical Products Group added $51.6 million of second-quarter sales and $189.3 million in the six months. With the deal closed on May 1, 2025, reported growth from the third quarter of 2026 should rest on the existing business.
Consensus expects FY26E revenue of $5.5 billion, up about 40%, then $6.4 billion in FY27E, a smaller step; our valuation turns on how the market prices that slowdown.

Management's 2026 objectives include growth through higher-growth verticals, new products and innovation, global expansion and acquisitions, and it says investment in new products has contributed to sales growth.

management.leadership: The March 2026 proxy names the 2025 executive team. Beth A. Wozniak is Chair and Chief Executive Officer. Gary Corona became Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer effective March 31, 2025, when Sara E. Zawoyski, the former CFO, became President of Systems Protection; Brian Coleman became President of Electrical Connections effective March 17, 2025. Lynnette Heath is Executive Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer, and Aravind Padmanabhan is Executive Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. The proxy describes the Spark management system, built on People, Growth, Lean, Digital and Velocity. The finance and segment leadership changed in early 2025, so the team's record in its current roles is short, though the organic growth since then is strong. The proxy's account of 2025 cash-flow growth rests on a basis the statement table does not match, as the cash-flow discussion explains.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation in 2025 turned on the portfolio. The Thermal Management sale and the Electrical Products Group purchase, both described in the overview, shifted nVent toward infrastructure. Shareholder returns came second: the FY25 buybacks and dividends discussed under cash flow exceeded the table's free cash flow but are small beside the share price. Management's 2026 objectives pair deploying capital strategically to drive growth and value creation with acquisitions and the integration of recent deals, so further acquisitions are likely to take priority over a higher payout. That suits a business growing this fast, but it adds integration risk and leaves holders relying on execution rather than yield.
management.governance: The source is the March 2026 proxy excerpt. All non-employee directors are independent, there is an independent Lead Director, and independent directors meet regularly without management present. The proxy cites over 99% average board meeting attendance, annual board and committee self-assessments, proxy access for director nominees, no poison pill, stock ownership requirements for officers and directors, and an insider trading policy with anti-hedging and anti-pledging provisions. The board oversees risks including artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. In its 2025 outreach nVent held calls with holders of approximately 12% of outstanding shares, measured on June 30, 2025 data. The Chair and Chief Executive Officer roles are combined, a structure the independent Lead Director partly offsets. The excerpt shows no red flags, but it carries no pay figures, so we do not judge executive compensation.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt sets stock ownership requirements for officers and directors but includes no ownership table, so we cannot state insider stakes or judge how closely management's interests track outside holders'.

idiosyncratic: Demand concentration: most second-quarter organic growth came from the infrastructure business, which holds the data-center business. A pause in data-center or power-utility capital spending would hit growth and, through lost SG&A leverage, the operating-margin gain.

Cost and tariff pressure: management expects inflationary cost increases, including impacts related to tariffs, to continue throughout 2026 and beyond, which it says could negatively impact results. The quarter's tariff reimbursements were offset by other incremental tariffs, so they gave no net relief.

Acquisition integration: the 10-Q's forward-looking statements name integrating the Electrical Products Group as a risk, and the 10-K warns that acquisitions can bring unforeseen liabilities, impairment charges and dilution. Further acquisitions are among management's 2026 objectives.
Valuation: a slowdown would likely cost both earnings and multiple at once; our Bear case prices that combination.
risks.systemic: The 10-K ties demand to the overall strength of the global economy, industrial and governmental capital spending, interest rates, inflation, and energy and commodity prices, and notes that many industrial customers are cyclical. nVent sells across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, India, Africa and Asia Pacific, and the 10-Q names volatility in currency exchange rates, interest rates and commodity prices, military conflicts and rapid changes in global trade policy among the factors that could move its results. These pressures would hit the sector broadly, not nVent alone, but a business priced for growth has less room to absorb them.

body: Our call is HOLD, with targets of $160 to $205. The operating story is strong and management's explanation of it is clear, but at $162.85 the price already sits close to what we think the shares are worth, with an expected upside of +7.3% against a bear-case downside of -21.1%.

On unchanged scenarios, a price modestly below today's would derive BUY, and a price near the $184.64 52-week high would derive SELL. Beyond price, we would move to BUY if later quarters show organic growth staying close to the second-quarter pace once the acquisition comparison has gone, with operating margin still rising, because that would argue for holding today's current-year multiple in the Base. We would move toward SELL if organic growth slows sharply while gross margin keeps falling, the combination our Bear case describes.
